From Optimum to Demand

INTERACTIVE WORKSHEET • UNIT 2.1
Learning Curve Collective
MICROECONOMICS • DEMAND
1

The upgrade: from one dot to the whole curve

In Unit 1 you solved problems like “$p_x = 3$, $m = 30$, find the bundle” — and the answer was one point. Unit 2 asks a bigger question: what does the consumer buy at every possible price? Answering it takes no new math — just a new interpretation. Before, $x^*$ came out as a single stationary number because $p_x$, $p_y$, and $m$ were all pinned down. Now run the exact same tangency-plus-budget (or kink, or corner) recipe, but leave $p_x$, $p_y$, $m$ as letters and imagine them free to move. The solution is the same — but the answer now changes as each variable changes. In particular, watch what happens to $x^*$ as $p_x$ rises: $x^*$ falls. That is the Law of Demand.

$$x^*(p_x,\, p_y,\, m) \;=\; \text{the } \textbf{demand function} \text{ for } x$$

Feed in any prices and income, and it spits out the optimal quantity. The demand curve is what you get when you graph $x^*$ against its own price $p_x$, holding $p_y$ and $m$ frozen (“ceteris paribus”). By convention economists put price on the vertical axis — blame Alfred Marshall.

Movement along vs. shift — the definition. The demand graph plots one relationship: how $x^*$ responds to its own price $p_x$. Because $p_x$ is already an axis of the graph, changing $p_x$ changes nothing about the curve — it only changes where on the curve you are. That is a movement along the demand curve. Everything else ($p_y$, $m$) is frozen background baked into the curve's position — so when one of those changes, the whole relationship between $p_x$ and $x^*$ has to be redrawn. That is a shift of the demand curve.

2

Intro econ's demand line — same two moves

Before deriving anything from utility, here is the demand curve the way an intro course hands it to you — already a straight line:

$$x^*(p_x,\, p_y,\, m) \;=\; 20 + \frac{m}{12} + 2p_y - 6p_x$$

Read the movement-vs-shift rule straight off the formula. The $-6p_x$ term is the slope relationship the graph draws: pick a $p_x$, get an $x^*$ — changing $p_x$ just picks a different point on the same line, and the negative sign in front is the Law of Demand (as $p_x$ rises, $x^*$ falls). The other two terms, $\tfrac{m}{12}$ and $2p_y$, are baked into the intercept: change $m$ or $p_y$ and the whole line is redrawn — a shift. At the baseline $m = 120$, $p_y = 2$ the line is $x^* = 34 - 6p_x$.

1

Cobb–Douglas demand: the share rule grows up

The shape

Concept
$$U = x^{a}y^{b} \;\Longrightarrow\; x^*(p_x, m) = \frac{a}{a+b}\cdot\frac{m}{p_x}, \qquad y^*(p_y, m) = \frac{b}{a+b}\cdot\frac{m}{p_y}$$

This is the share rule from Unit 1, now wearing its real name: a demand function. Two features to memorize because exams love them: demand for $x$ does not contain $p_y$ (cross-price effect is exactly zero — a Cobb–Douglas quirk), and it is proportional to income (double $m$, double every purchase).

Worked example

Worked Example
Given
  • $U = x^{2}y^{3}$ — leave $p_x$, $p_y$, $m$ as letters
  • Find the demand functions $x^*(p_x, m)$ and $y^*(p_y, m)$, then trace the demand curve for $m = 50$ at $p_x = 2, 4, 5$.
1

Tangency with letters. MRS $= \dfrac{a}{b}\cdot\dfrac{y}{x} = \dfrac{2y}{3x}$, so

$$\frac{2y}{3x} = \frac{p_x}{p_y} \;\Longrightarrow\; y = \frac{3p_x}{2p_y}\,x$$

2

Into the budget $p_x x + p_y y = m$ — watch $p_y$ cancel:

$$p_x x + p_y\!\left(\frac{3p_x}{2p_y}x\right) = p_x x + \frac{3}{2}p_x x = \frac{5}{2}\,p_x x = m$$

3

Solve for $x$ — this is the demand function:

$$x^*(p_x, m) = \frac{2m}{5p_x}, \qquad y^*(p_y, m) = \frac{3m}{5p_y}$$

Exactly the share rule: fractions $\tfrac{2}{5}$ and $\tfrac{3}{5}$ of income, divided by own price.

4

Trace the curve at $m = 50$: $\;x^* = \dfrac{20}{p_x}$.

$$p_x = 2 \Rightarrow x^* = 10, \qquad p_x = 4 \Rightarrow x^* = 5, \qquad p_x = 5 \Rightarrow x^* = 4$$

Three dots on the same demand curve — in Unit 1 each one would have been a whole separate problem.

Where the weights go: $a$ and $b$ survive only as the income share $\tfrac{a}{a+b}$. They never multiply the price. Note $p_y$ vanished in step 2 — that cancellation is the zero cross-price result.

Your turn

Practice
Given — Problem 1
  • $U = x^{3/5}y^{2/5}$. Derive $x^*(p_x, m)$, then evaluate at $m = 25$ for $p_x = 3, 5, 15$.

Share of good $x$ is $\dfrac{3/5}{3/5+2/5} = \dfrac{3}{5}$, so $x^* = \dfrac{3m}{5p_x}$. At $m=25$: $x^* = \dfrac{15}{p_x}$.

$$p_x = 3 \Rightarrow 5, \qquad p_x = 5 \Rightarrow 3, \qquad p_x = 15 \Rightarrow 1$$

Given — Problem 2
  • $U = x^{2}y^{2}$. Derive $x^*(p_x, m)$ and evaluate at $m = 40$ for $p_x = 2, 4, 10$. Does $p_y$ appear anywhere?

Equal weights $\Rightarrow$ share $\tfrac{1}{2}$: $\;x^* = \dfrac{m}{2p_x}$. At $m=40$: $x^* = \dfrac{20}{p_x} \Rightarrow 10,\ 5,\ 2$. No $p_y$ anywhere — Cobb–Douglas cross-price effects are zero.

$$\boxed{x^* = \tfrac{m}{2p_x}}$$

2

From formula to picture

You just derived $x^*(p_x, m) = \dfrac{2m}{5p_x}$ for $U = x^2y^3$. Read the formula like a forecast of the graph: $p_x$ sits in the denominator, so as $p_x$ rises, $x^*$ falls — the Law of Demand, straight from the algebra. $m$ sits in the numerator, so more income drags the whole curve outward — a shift. And $p_y$ vanished during the algebra, so for Cobb–Douglas the other price can't shift anything at all.

3

Same demand function, $x^* = \dfrac{2m}{5p_x}$. Drag $p_x$ to move along; drag $m$ to shift (dashed ghost = the $m=120$ curve). Then try $p_y$ — and watch nothing happen.

Quasilinear demand: income drops out

The shape

Concept
$$U = A\sqrt{x} + By \;\Longrightarrow\; x^*(p_x, p_y) = \left(\frac{A\,p_y}{2B\,p_x}\right)^{\!2} \qquad (\text{no } m \text{ anywhere})$$

Unit 1's “settled appetite” becomes a demand function with a missing ingredient: income is not an argument. Tangency alone pins down $x^*$, so richer and poorer consumers with these preferences buy the same $x$ — every extra dollar flows to $y$. (Fine print: this needs $m$ large enough to afford $x^*$ in the first place; we'll stay in that region.)

Worked example

Worked Example
Given
  • $U = 12\sqrt{x} + 2y$ — keep $p_x$, $p_y$, $m$ as letters
  • Find $x^*(p_x, p_y)$, then trace the demand curve for $p_y = 2$ at $p_x = 2, 3, 6$. Finally get $y^*$ at $m = 40$, $p_x = 2$.
1

Marginal utilities. $MU_x = \dfrac{6}{\sqrt{x}}$, $\;MU_y = 2$, so MRS $= \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{x}}$ — the weight on $y$ has been divided out.

2

Tangency with letters:

$$\frac{3}{\sqrt{x}} = \frac{p_x}{p_y} \;\Longrightarrow\; \sqrt{x} = \frac{3p_y}{p_x} \;\Longrightarrow\; x^*(p_x, p_y) = \frac{9p_y^2}{p_x^2}$$

Income never entered — the budget wasn't needed to find $x^*$.

3

Trace the curve at $p_y = 2$: $\;x^* = \dfrac{36}{p_x^2}$.

$$p_x = 2 \Rightarrow 9, \qquad p_x = 3 \Rightarrow 4, \qquad p_x = 6 \Rightarrow 1$$

4

$y^*$ mops up the budget. At $m = 40$, $p_x = 2$: spending on $x$ is $2 \times 9 = 18$, so $y^* = \dfrac{40 - 18}{2} = 11$.

Signature to quote on exams: quasilinear demand for $x$ depends only on the price ratio — raise $m$ by \$100 and $x^*$ doesn't budge; all \$100 lands on $y$. This is why quasilinear preferences make consumer surplus clean later in the course.

Your turn

Practice
Given — Problem 1
  • $U = 16\sqrt{x} + 4y$. Derive $x^*(p_x, p_y)$, then evaluate at $p_y = 4$ for $p_x = 2, 4, 8$.

$MU_x = \dfrac{8}{\sqrt{x}}$, $MU_y = 4 \Rightarrow$ MRS $= \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{x}} = \dfrac{p_x}{p_y} \Rightarrow x^* = \left(\dfrac{2p_y}{p_x}\right)^2$. At $p_y = 4$: $x^* = \dfrac{64}{p_x^2} \Rightarrow 16,\ 4,\ 1$.

$$\boxed{x^* = \left(\tfrac{2p_y}{p_x}\right)^{2}}$$

Given — Problem 2
  • $U = 10\ln x + 2y$. Derive $x^*(p_x, p_y)$ and evaluate at $p_y = 2$ for $p_x = 2, 5, 10$. (Recall $\frac{d}{dx}\ln x = \frac{1}{x}$.)

$MU_x = \dfrac{10}{x}$, $MU_y = 2 \Rightarrow$ MRS $= \dfrac{5}{x} = \dfrac{p_x}{p_y} \Rightarrow x^* = \dfrac{5p_y}{p_x}$. At $p_y = 2$: $x^* = \dfrac{10}{p_x} \Rightarrow 5,\ 2,\ 1$.

$$\boxed{x^* = \tfrac{5p_y}{p_x}}$$

2

From formula to picture

You just derived $x^*(p_x, p_y) = \dfrac{9p_y^2}{p_x^2}$ for $U = 12\sqrt{x} + 2y$. Read it like a forecast of the graph: $p_x$ sits in the denominator squared, so as $p_x$ rises, $x^*$ falls fast — the Law of Demand with extra bite. $p_y$ sits in the numerator, so a pricier $y$ pushes the whole curve outward — a shift. And $m$ is simply not in the formula — income cannot shift this curve, no matter how rich the consumer gets.

3

This is the worked example above: $U = 12\sqrt{x} + 2y \Rightarrow x^* = \dfrac{9p_y^2}{p_x^2}$. Drag $p_x$ to move along; drag $p_y$ to shift. Then drag $m$ — the curve doesn’t care how rich you are.

Complements demand: both prices matter

The shape

Concept
$$U = \min(a x,\, b y) \;\Longrightarrow\; x^* = \frac{b\,m}{b\,p_x + a\,p_y}, \qquad y^* = \frac{a\,m}{b\,p_x + a\,p_y}$$

The cheat-sheet formulas from Unit 1, reread as demand functions. Contrast with Cobb–Douglas: here $p_y$ does appear in the demand for $x$ — a pricier partner good drags your purchases of $x$ down with it (negative cross-price effect, the defining mark of complements). Demand is still proportional to $m$.

Worked example

Worked Example
Given
  • $U = \min(3x,\, 2y)$ — keep prices and income as letters
  • Find $x^*(p_x, p_y, m)$ and $y^*$, then trace the demand curve for $p_y = 2$, $m = 24$ at $p_x = 1, 3, 9$.
1

No waste, with letters: $3x = 2y \Rightarrow y = \dfrac{3}{2}x$.

2

Into the budget $p_x x + p_y y = m$:

$$p_x x + p_y\!\left(\tfrac{3}{2}x\right) = \left(p_x + \tfrac{3}{2}p_y\right)x = m \;\Longrightarrow\; x^* = \frac{2m}{2p_x + 3p_y}$$

and $y^* = \tfrac{3}{2}x^* = \dfrac{3m}{2p_x + 3p_y}$. Matches the general formula with $a = 3$, $b = 2$ — crossed weights, as always.

3

Trace the curve at $p_y = 2$, $m = 24$: $\;x^* = \dfrac{48}{2p_x + 6} = \dfrac{24}{p_x + 3}$.

$$p_x = 1 \Rightarrow x^* = 6\ (y^* = 9), \qquad p_x = 3 \Rightarrow 4\ (6), \qquad p_x = 9 \Rightarrow 2\ (3)$$

Reading the denominator: $2p_x + 3p_y$ is (twice) the cost of a “serving bundle.” Raising either price shrinks demand for both goods — try it in the Curves & Shifts tab and watch the whole curve slide inward when $p_y$ rises.

Your turn

Practice
Given — Problem 1
  • $U = \min(2x,\, 3y)$. Derive $x^*(p_x, p_y, m)$, then evaluate at $p_y = 3$, $m = 40$ for $p_x = 2, 3, 8$.

No waste: $2x = 3y \Rightarrow y = \tfrac{2}{3}x$. Budget: $\left(p_x + \tfrac{2}{3}p_y\right)x = m \Rightarrow x^* = \dfrac{3m}{3p_x + 2p_y}$. At $p_y=3$, $m=40$: $x^* = \dfrac{120}{3p_x + 6} = \dfrac{40}{p_x + 2} \Rightarrow 10,\ 8,\ 4$.

$$\boxed{x^* = \tfrac{3m}{3p_x + 2p_y}}$$

Given — Problem 2
  • $U = \min(4x,\, 2y)$. Derive both demand functions, then evaluate at $p_y = 2$, $m = 36$ for $p_x = 2, 5, 8$.

No waste: $4x = 2y \Rightarrow y = 2x$. Budget: $(p_x + 2p_y)x = m \Rightarrow x^* = \dfrac{m}{p_x + 2p_y}$, $\;y^* = \dfrac{2m}{p_x + 2p_y}$. At $p_y=2$, $m=36$: $x^* = \dfrac{36}{p_x+4} \Rightarrow 6, 4, 3$ with $y^* = 12, 8, 6$.

$$\boxed{x^* = \tfrac{m}{p_x + 2p_y}, \quad y^* = 2x^*}$$

2

From formula to picture

You just derived $x^*(p_x, p_y, m) = \dfrac{2m}{2p_x + 3p_y}$ for $U = \min(3x, 2y)$. Read the forecast: $p_x$ in the denominator — as it rises, $x^*$ falls, the Law of Demand. $m$ in the numerator — more income shifts the curve outward. But unlike Cobb–Douglas, $p_y$ survived the algebra, and it sits in the denominator: a pricier partner good drags demand for $x$ inward. Negative cross-price effect — the complements signature.

3

Drag it yourself

The worked example: $U = \min(3x, 2y) \Rightarrow x^* = \dfrac{2m}{2p_x + 3p_y}$. Drag $p_x$ to move along. Then shift it two ways: $m$ pushes the curve out, and $p_y$ — the price of the partner good — drags it inward. Both prices matter.

Substitutes demand: the cliff

The shape

Concept
$$U = a x + b y \;\Longrightarrow\; x^* = \begin{cases} \dfrac{m}{p_x} & \text{if } p_x < \dfrac{a}{b}\,p_y \\[6pt] \text{any } x \in \left[0, \tfrac{m}{p_x}\right] & \text{if } p_x = \dfrac{a}{b}\,p_y \\[6pt] 0 & \text{if } p_x > \dfrac{a}{b}\,p_y \end{cases}$$

Corner logic, priced out: good $x$ wins the whole budget whenever $\tfrac{a}{p_x} > \tfrac{b}{p_y}$, which rearranges to $p_x < \tfrac{a}{b}p_y$. So demand is all-or-nothing with a cliff at the threshold price $p_x = \tfrac{a}{b}p_y$. Below the cliff the curve is the hyperbola $m/p_x$; above it, demand is zero. Cross-price effect is positive — a pricier rival sends buyers to $x$ — the defining mark of substitutes.

Worked example

Worked Example
Given
  • $U = 3x + 2y$, $\;p_y = 2$, $\;m = 12$
  • Find the threshold price for $p_x$ and the full demand curve; evaluate at $p_x = 1, 2, 4$.
1

Threshold. Good $x$ wins when $\dfrac{3}{p_x} > \dfrac{2}{p_y} = 1$, i.e. when

$$p_x < \frac{a}{b}\,p_y = \frac{3}{2}(2) = 3$$

2

Demand curve, piece by piece: below \$3, spend everything on $x$: $x^* = \dfrac{12}{p_x}$. Above \$3, $x^* = 0$. Exactly at \$3, any bundle on the budget line ties.

3

Evaluate:

$$p_x = 1 \Rightarrow x^* = 12, \qquad p_x = 2 \Rightarrow x^* = 6, \qquad p_x = 4 \Rightarrow x^* = 0$$

Between $p_x = 2$ and $p_x = 4$ the consumer went from six units to none — that's the cliff.

Exam trap: the threshold is $\tfrac{a}{b}p_y$, weights in that order — it comes from rearranging $\tfrac{a}{p_x} = \tfrac{b}{p_y}$. Flipping it puts the cliff in the wrong place and every answer below follows the wrong branch.

Your turn

Practice
Given — Problem 1
  • $U = 2x + 5y$, $\;p_y = 10$, $\;m = 20$. Find the threshold and evaluate $x^*$ at $p_x = 2, 4, 5$.

Threshold: $\tfrac{a}{b}p_y = \tfrac{2}{5}(10) = 4$. So $p_x = 2 < 4 \Rightarrow x^* = \tfrac{20}{2} = 10$; $\;p_x = 4 \Rightarrow$ tie (any bundle on the line); $\;p_x = 5 > 4 \Rightarrow x^* = 0$.

$$\boxed{\text{cliff at } p_x = 4}$$

Given — Problem 2
  • $U = 6x + 4y$, $\;p_y = 2$, $\;m = 18$. Find the threshold and evaluate $x^*$ at $p_x = 2, 3, 4$. Then: if $p_y$ rises to $4$, where does the cliff move?

Threshold: $\tfrac{6}{4}(2) = 3$. So $x^*(2) = 9$; $x^*(3)$ = tie; $x^*(4) = 0$. If $p_y \to 4$: cliff moves to $\tfrac{6}{4}(4) = 6$ — the demand curve for $x$ shifts out when the rival gets pricier (positive cross-price effect).

$$\boxed{\text{cliff at } 3 \to 6}$$

2

From formula to picture

The demand you derived is a two-piece formula: $x^* = \dfrac{m}{p_x}$ below the cliff at $p_x = \tfrac{3}{2}p_y$, and $x^* = 0$ above it. Forecast: along the hyperbola, $p_x$ in the denominator gives the Law of Demand — until you cross the threshold and demand doesn’t just fall, it vanishes. $m$ rescales the hyperbola but cannot move the cliff. The cliff’s location is $\tfrac{3}{2}p_y$, so a pricier rival raises it — positive cross-price effect, the substitutes signature.

3

Drag it yourself

The worked example: $U = 3x + 2y$, so the cliff sits at $p_x = \tfrac{3}{2}p_y$. Below the cliff demand is the hyperbola $m/p_x$; above it, zero. Drag $p_x$ across the cliff and watch the dot jump. $m$ resizes the hyperbola; a pricier rival ($p_y$ up) pushes the cliff higher — positive cross-price, the substitutes signature.

What to notice: Cobb–Douglas ignores $p_y$ completely (zero cross-price). Quasilinear ignores $m$ completely (zero income effect on $x$). Complements shift inward when $p_y$ rises; substitutes shift the cliff outward. One slider-minute here is worth a page of memorization.

1

Mixed practice

Eight problems, shuffled on every load, type hidden until you open the solution. Routine: name the type from the utility function, derive the demand function with letters, and only then plug in numbers.

1

Derive $x^*(p_x, m)$ for $U = x^{1/4}y^{3/4}$, then evaluate at $m = 48$ for $p_x = 2, 4, 6$.

Cobb–Douglas

Share of $x$ is $\tfrac{1}{4}$: $x^* = \dfrac{m}{4p_x}$. At $m=48$: $x^* = \dfrac{12}{p_x} \Rightarrow 6,\ 3,\ 2$.

$$\boxed{x^* = \tfrac{m}{4p_x}}$$

2

Derive $x^*(p_x, p_y, m)$ for $U = \min(5x, 2y)$, then evaluate at $p_y = 2$, $m = 60$ for $p_x = 1, 5, 7$.

Perfect Complements

No waste $5x = 2y \Rightarrow y = \tfrac{5}{2}x$. Budget: $\left(p_x + \tfrac{5}{2}p_y\right)x = m \Rightarrow x^* = \dfrac{2m}{2p_x + 5p_y}$. At $p_y=2$, $m=60$: $x^* = \dfrac{120}{2p_x+10} = \dfrac{60}{p_x+5} \Rightarrow 10,\ 6,\ 5$.

$$\boxed{x^* = \tfrac{2m}{2p_x + 5p_y}}$$

3

Derive $x^*(p_x, p_y)$ for $U = 20\sqrt{x} + 5y$, then evaluate at $p_y = 4$ for $p_x = 2, 4, 8$. Why is $m$ missing from your formula?

Quasilinear

$MU_x = \dfrac{10}{\sqrt{x}}$, $MU_y = 5 \Rightarrow$ MRS $= \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{x}} = \dfrac{p_x}{p_y} \Rightarrow x^* = \left(\dfrac{2p_y}{p_x}\right)^2$. At $p_y=4$: $x^* = \dfrac{64}{p_x^2} \Rightarrow 16,\ 4,\ 1$. $m$ is missing because tangency alone pins down $x^*$ — income only decides how much $y$ is left over.

$$\boxed{x^* = \left(\tfrac{2p_y}{p_x}\right)^2}$$

4

Find the full demand curve for $U = 4x + 3y$ with $p_y = 6$, $m = 32$, and evaluate $x^*$ at $p_x = 4, 8, 10$.

Perfect Substitutes

Threshold: $\tfrac{a}{b}p_y = \tfrac{4}{3}(6) = 8$. Below it $x^* = \tfrac{32}{p_x}$, above it $x^* = 0$. So $x^*(4) = 8$; $x^*(8)$ = tie (any bundle on the line); $x^*(10) = 0$.

$$\boxed{\text{cliff at } p_x = 8}$$

5

Shift or movement? For $U = x^2y^3$ with $p_x = 2$: income rises from $m = 50$ to $m = 75$. Compute $x^*$ before and after, and say precisely what happened to the demand curve.

Cobb–Douglas — Shift

$x^* = \dfrac{2m}{5p_x} = \dfrac{m}{5}$ at $p_x = 2$: so $10 \to 15$. Because $m$ changed (not $p_x$), the entire curve shifted outward — at every price the consumer now buys 1.5× as much. Movement along would require a change in $p_x$ itself.

$$\boxed{x^*: 10 \to 15 \text{ (outward shift)}}$$

6

Concept check. A consumer's demand for coffee is completely unchanged after a \$200/month raise. Which utility type is consistent with this, and which feature of its demand function explains it?

Quasilinear — Concept

Quasilinear, $U = v(x) + By$. Its demand $x^*(p_x, p_y)$ has no $m$ in it — tangency $v'(x) = \tfrac{B\,p_x}{p_y}$ solves $x^*$ from prices alone, so the whole raise flows into the other good. (Preview: in 2.2 language, the income effect on $x$ is zero.)

7

Both demands at once. For $U = \min(2x, 5y)$, derive $x^*$ and $y^*$ as functions of $(p_x, p_y, m)$, then evaluate at $p_x = 2$, $p_y = 5$, $m = 40$.

Perfect Complements

$x^* = \dfrac{5m}{5p_x + 2p_y}$, $\;y^* = \dfrac{2m}{5p_x + 2p_y}$ (weights crossed). At $(2, 5, 40)$: denominator $= 10 + 10 = 20$, so $x^* = 10$, $y^* = 4$. Check: $\min(20, 20) = 20$, budget $2(10) + 5(4) = 40$ ✓.

$$\boxed{(x^*, y^*) = (10,\ 4)}$$

8

Cross-price detective. For $U = \min(2x, 3y)$ with $p_x = 2$, $m = 40$: compute $x^*$ at $p_y = 3$ and at $p_y = 9$. What sign is the cross-price effect, and what sign would it be for perfect substitutes?

Complements — Cross-Price

$x^* = \dfrac{3m}{3p_x + 2p_y} = \dfrac{120}{6 + 2p_y}$: at $p_y = 3$, $x^* = 10$; at $p_y = 9$, $x^* = 5$. Rival… rather, partner good got pricier and demand for $x$ fell: cross-price effect is negative for complements. For substitutes it's positive — a pricier rival pushes the cliff outward and sends buyers to $x$.

$$\boxed{x^*: 10 \to 5 \;(\text{negative cross-price})}$$

★

Demand functions at a glance

Cobb–Douglas — smooth

$$U = x^a y^b \Rightarrow x^* = \frac{a}{a+b}\cdot\frac{m}{p_x}$$

Fixed income share. No $p_y$ (zero cross-price). Proportional to $m$. Shifted by: $m$ only.

Quasilinear — income-proof

$$U = A\sqrt{x} + By \Rightarrow x^* = \left(\frac{A p_y}{2B p_x}\right)^{2}$$

($\ln$ version: $U = A\ln x + By \Rightarrow x^* = \frac{A p_y}{B p_x}$.) No $m$ at all. Shifted by: $p_y$ only.

Perfect complements — both prices

$$U = \min(ax, by) \Rightarrow x^* = \frac{b\,m}{b p_x + a p_y}$$

Weights crossed in the answer. Negative cross-price. Shifted by: $m$ and $p_y$.

Perfect substitutes — the cliff

$$U = ax + by \Rightarrow x^* = \frac{m}{p_x} \text{ if } p_x < \tfrac{a}{b}p_y, \text{ else } 0$$

All-or-nothing at threshold $\tfrac{a}{b}p_y$. Positive cross-price: $p_y\!\uparrow$ moves the cliff out. Shifted by: $m$ and $p_y$.

ChangeEffect on the demand curve for $x$
$p_x$ changesMovement along the curve — never a shift
$m$ risesShifts out for Cobb–Douglas, complements, substitutes; no effect for quasilinear
$p_y$ risesNo effect for Cobb–Douglas; shifts in for complements; shifts the cliff out for substitutes; shifts out for quasilinear ($\sqrt{\ }$ and $\ln$ forms)

Universal workflow: identify the type from the utility function → run the Unit 1 recipe with $p_x, p_y, m$ as letters → the expression for $x^*$ is the demand function → plug in numbers last. If your “demand function” still has an $x$ or $y$ in it, you stopped too early.

→

Why does the Law of Demand work?

Every curve in this sheet obeyed the same rule: $p_x$ up, $x^*$ down. But why? A price rise actually does two different things to you at once, and the next lesson pulls them apart:

  • Substitution effect: $x$ just got relatively more expensive than $y$, so you swap some $x$ for $y$ — even if your purchasing power were somehow protected.
  • Income effect: nobody protects your purchasing power. The same $m$ now buys less, so you're effectively poorer — and you cut back on normal goods, $x$ included.

The picture below splits the move from old bundle $A$ to new bundle $C$ into exactly those two steps, using a compensated budget (gold, dashed) that pivots to the new prices but through the old bundle: $A \rightarrow B$ is pure substitution, $B \rightarrow C$ is pure income.

Drag the new price of $x$ — above or below the old price of $1$ — and watch the two effects split apart and change sign together. ($U = x^2y^3$, $p_y = 1$, $m = 50$.) One thing that will not move: the $y$-coordinate of $A$ and $C$ — Cobb–Douglas demand for $y$ ignores $p_x$ entirely (the zero cross-price effect from this very sheet). Only the detour bundle $B$ climbs in $y$.
